sentences.text: Like typical diplodocids, Supersaurus had a small skull, sturdy legs, and long neck and tail.
Supersaurus had a slightly less robust build than Apatosaurus and possessed much longer cervical vertebrae, resulting in a proportionally longer neck.
The WDC DMJ-021 specimen shows that Supersaurus was similar to Apatosaurus but less robust, with exceptionally long neck vertebrae.
Anatomically, Supersaurus was very similar to Apatosaurus, featuring a robust and deep chest due to wide ribs and a thickened neck.
Michael Benton agreed that the BYU 9024 vertebra belongs to Supersaurus, suggesting the animal could reach 50 meters in length.
Supersaurus is among the largest diplodocids and is possibly the longest sauropod known from well-preserved remains.
Mass estimates for the known Supersaurus specimens range from 35 to 44 metric tons.
Despite unreliable dating methods, the "Jimbo" specimen is considered possibly the oldest known dinosaur.
The type species, Supersaurus vivianae, was first discovered by Vivian Jones in Colorado in 1972.
The original fossil remains of Supersaurus were found at the Dry Mesa Quarry in 1972.
The first remains of Supersaurus consisted of a few bones, including a 2.4-meter-long scapulocoracoid holotype and some neck vertebrae found in the Morrison Formation of Colorado, USA.
A more complete specimen nicknamed "Jimbo" was discovered in Converse County, Wyoming, USA.
Paleontologist James A. Jensen described Supersaurus and designated a scapulocoracoid (originally labeled BYU 5500) as the type specimen.
The genus Supersaurus was formally described by James A. Jensen in 1985.
The name "Supersaurus" was used informally from 1973 but was not officially published until 1985.
Supersaurus belongs to the family Diplodocidae.
The parent group of Supersaurus is Diplodocinae.

Most studies initially placed Supersaurus in the subfamily Diplodocinae due to its relation to Barosaurus, but later research based on the WDC DMJ-021 specimen reclassified it as a close relative of Apatosaurus within the subfamily Apatosaurinae.
Supersaurus has had several synonyms including Dystylosaurus, Ultrasauros, Dinehirosaurus, and Jensenosaurus.
The name Ultrasauros is now considered a junior synonym of Supersaurus because Supersaurus was named first.
The genus Dystylosaurus is now considered a junior synonym of Supersaurus.
The type species of the genus Supersaurus is Supersaurus vivianae.
Supersaurus lived in North America during the Late Jurassic period.
The fossils of Supersaurus date between 153 and 145 million years ago.
Supersaurus lived during the late Jurassic period, approximately 155.7 to 150.8 million years ago, in what is now North America and possibly Europe.
Supersaurus lived from the Kimmeridgian to the Tithonian stages, between 154.8 and 143.1 million years ago.
